messages.author: dfe68e390fa72e44
messages.subject: pcountOpen: independence of samples
parts:
Hello,

I am exploring effects of environmental variables on Group size in Asian elephants. I want to estimate group sizes in each site taking into account that there is a variation due to elephants joining and/or leaving the group. I also want to take into account the detectability. The data I have was taken from opportunistic observations of elephants and counting the number of elephants in each site at time i and then again at time i+1, x+2, x+3 ... x+n. All measurements were made for each site the same day but over a different length of time that varied between sites from several minutes to a few hours. For each site I have environmental variables.

So I want to ask if pcountOpen can be a good way to analyze my data?

I am also worried by the separation between time 1 to time x+1 which is currently 10 minutes, which I think make my observations not independent. Is that a big problem for the analysis?

Thank you very much for any comment or suggestion.

Julie.

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] pcountOpen: independence of samples
parts:
hi Julie,
 I think the short interval between counts is a big problem for interpreting the results from this model and I wouldn't recommend using it in this case without having  good specific reasons for doing so.  One possible argument to make: you could interpret the recruitment and mortality rate parameters from the Dail-Madsen model as being directly related to movement into and out of each site if that might be a meaningful interpretation in the context (I have no idea if it is).
 regards
andy

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] pcountOpen: independence of samples
parts:
Hello Julie:

If I am am understanding your goal correctly, I think you will likely violate an assumption of the Dail-Madsen Model (manuscript text below).

"Second, the number of animals surviving and staying at a site will not be a binomial random variable if clusters of animals survive or emigrate together. Royle (2008) gives a framework for modeling the effect of cluster size in wildlife surveys, which relaxes the binomial assumption, and it may be possible to apply these models to the setting considered here. However, these models require auxiliary information beyond the observed counts, such as distance sampling or double- observer sampling, so extending this framework to include the generalized model is an open research question." Dail and Madsen 2010 on page 9.



I think that elephant group size will affect detection which in your case is a metric of interest. I am sure others will have suggestions too. But I would consider alternative approaches.


Good luck,

James Martin
